title: Lawyer 3.0 and the Milkshake Test: Ray Brescia on Legal AI, Client Value, and the Next Wave of Lawyering
author: Ray Brescia

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Brescia aligns with adjacent cluster themes: AI can accelerate preliminary legal work, requires human verification, and may shift work in-house under client pressure for efficiency. However, he does not address the cluster’s central proposition that automation weakens apprenticeship and partner-succession routes, nor its proposed responses of explicit training funding, simulation, feedback and broader careers.
qs: That’s all it’s good for right now, not last drafts.
I use these tools every day, usually as an outline or to answer a quick question, but I always double-check because it’s often a tick or two off.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s workflow-centred procurement proposition and materially develops it with a structured process spanning market analysis, evaluation, use cases, pilots and requirements. However, it describes Legal Technology Hub’s guidance resources rather than demonstrating realized adoption, performance or renewal value.
qs: We’ve been pulling together comprehensive guides for every step of the procurement process.
For each premium category, we have a landscape overview, an evaluation framework, a use case, a pilot guide, a requirements template, and then any other information we think is important.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Brescia accepts that legal AI’s value depends on human and organisational preparation, and materially develops the cluster’s adaptation agenda by specifying technological literacy and lawyer–engineer partnerships—rather than universal coding instruction—as the appropriate model.
qs: I think students should partner with people who code, and educate engineers on how law offices work and what ethical obligations lawyers have.
Lawyers should understand what the technology can do.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: Brescia accepts that legal GenAI may make work faster and less costly, while stressing that hallucinations persist even in commercial legal-research systems and that uncritical reliance can place fabricated authorities into filings. This supports the cluster’s core reliability proposition, though the source offers no quantitative evidence or developed analysis of verification’s net productivity cost.
qs: But we can look for efficiencies, make work go faster, be less costly to clients.
Research shows even the databases maintained by commercial legal research companies that use AI can hallucinate.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source directly supports selective augmentation: AI is useful for outlines and rapid first-pass work, but its outputs require checking and should not be treated as finished products. It also endorses beginning with familiar material so lawyers can identify errors. Its evidence is anecdotal and does not materially address the cluster’s junior-development or staffing-leverage tension.
qs: I use these tools every day, usually as an outline or to answer a quick question, but I always double-check because it’s often a tick or two off.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Brescia directly supports the cluster’s core view that AI will restructure legal-service production and delivery rather than eliminate lawyers. He describes bounded first-draft uses requiring human checking, alongside technology-enabled insourcing, commoditised services and scaled delivery to unmet markets. His disruptive-innovation framing is more bullish about longer-term market expansion, but does not conflict with the cluster’s cautious, hybrid model.
qs: The legal profession isn’t dead, but it is changing.
That’s all it’s good for right now, not last drafts.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: Wilkins directly supports the cluster’s proposition that a fast-changing legal-tech market requires disciplined, workflow-oriented research and procurement guidance. She describes structured evaluation and implementation resources while appropriately stopping short of claiming proven adoption, productivity or procurement outcomes.
qs: At the same time, the legal tech industry is changing so fast in the age of AI.
For each premium category, we have a landscape overview, an evaluation framework, a use case, a pilot guide, a requirements template, and then any other information we think is important.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Brescia supports the cluster’s central proposition that legal AI can improve speed and cost on suitable tasks but must remain within a human-led workflow. His position particularly reinforces verification as a competence obligation: lawyers must independently confirm that authorities exist and support the stated propositions before relying on AI output. His contribution is narrower than the full cluster, focusing primarily on hallucinations, professional responsibility and client pressure rather than broader operating-model redesign.
qs: You can use these tools as a head start, an outline, some arguments, maybe even cases you wouldn’t find otherwise, but you have to do the background research and make sure it’s accurate.
You need to check that the laws you’re citing exist, the cases are real, and they say what you say they say.

kp.k: Lawyer 3.0 frames technological change as institutional transformation
kp.d: Brescia argues that the profession is at an inflection point comparable to the transition from Lawyer 1.0 to Lawyer 2.0 around the turn of the 19th to the 20th century. His historical account connects technological and economic change to corporate law firms and greater efficiency, while linking professional institutions and more expensive entry requirements to elite responses to a diversifying bar. He predicts significant change from generative AI and predictive analytics rather than presenting measured evidence of current restructuring.
qs: The idea is that I believe we are at a critical inflection point in the profession.
Lawyers had to ramp up efficiency. They formed law firms to provide services to corporate clients.
So we transformed the practice of law, partly because of changes in technology, but also immigration and urbanization.
But now, I think generative AI and predictive analytics are going to make a significant change to the practice of law.

kp.k: Client value depends on jobs, not professional inputs
kp.d: Brescia applies Clayton Christensen’s jobs-to-be-done framework, illustrated by the milkshake study, to legal services: clients hire lawyers to solve problems rather than to obtain a lawyer for its own sake. Lambert adds that clients may understand these as business, personal or family problems rather than legal ones; Brescia agrees. The framework is an analogy for service design and client value, not empirical evidence of AI outcomes.
qs: So the idea is, what were customers hiring a milkshake to do? What problem were they trying to solve? That’s the jobs-to-be-done framework.
Customers, clients of lawyers, what are they hiring a lawyer to do? Solve their legal problem. Not to have a lawyer for the sake of having a lawyer.
A customer or client wants their business problem solved, or their border dispute with their neighbor, like a property line dispute.

kp.k: Recognizing legal need is part of service delivery
kp.d: Brescia argues that Lawyer 3.0 includes helping people recognize when their problems have legal dimensions. He cites Rebecca Sandefur’s research, without study details, as showing that people may not recognize legal problems or may turn to friends, neighbors or religious explanations. He qualifies this recommendation by noting that recognition alone may not help people who cannot afford or access a lawyer.
qs: One of the issues that accompanies that is laypeople don’t always realize they have a legal problem, or a problem a lawyer can solve.
It may not be great to explain they have a legal problem if they can’t afford a lawyer, don’t know how to access a lawyer, or only know a friend of a friend who knows a lawyer.
So getting people to understand they have a legal problem is a task of Lawyer 3.0.

kp.k: Productization offers tiered alternatives to bespoke legal services
kp.d: Brescia recommends developing standardized products and triaging clients into them, with more expensive bespoke services available when needed. He challenges the profession’s self-description as wholly bespoke by observing that lawyers already adapt previous work. His proposed model requires explaining the risks and adequacy of lower-cost options; it is a service-design recommendation rather than a demonstrated pricing result.
qs: But what lawyers often do is say, Mary’s case is a lot like Maureen’s case from three weeks ago. Let me start with what I did for Maureen, change the names, and work from there.
One way to reframe how lawyers operate, to make practice more efficient and effective, is to have products and triage clients to meet the products you have.

You can present options: a product that is less expensive than the one with all the bells and whistles, and should satisfy most needs adequately. Here are the risks. Or we can develop a bespoke approach, and here’s what it costs.

kp.k: Expert systems automate straightforward matters and escalate exceptions
kp.d: Brescia presents Pro Bono Net’s Citizenship Works as an existing example of productized legal assistance: it assesses citizenship eligibility, identifies barriers and generates applications when no red flags arise. He describes referral to an immigration lawyer when issues exceed the system’s capabilities, conditional on accurate and honest user answers. He anticipates broader 'TurboTaxification' and argues that high upfront expert-system costs can be recovered through volume over time; this example is not described as generative AI.
qs: Citizenship Works walks people through applying for citizenship. It goes through steps, assessing whether somebody is eligible to apply for citizenship, whether there are barriers, and it generates the application if there are no red flags.
Building those expert systems is expensive up front, but they have a long tail, and you make it up over time with volume.

If a user raises red flags in their application, the system sees that, and as long as the person is answering accurately and honestly, it identifies the red flags and says, hey, you need to talk to an immigration lawyer.

kp.k: Limited representation requires reasonable scope and informed consent
kp.d: Brescia distinguishes established limited-scope representation from productization, using housing-court lawyer-for-the-day programs as an example. He says scope must be reasonable, explained and accepted through informed consent, with judges generally made aware. He contrasts settlement assistance with an unreasonable hypothetical criminal-defense engagement that ends on the eve of trial if plea negotiations fail. His guiding recommendation is that assistance should not leave clients worse off; the discussion does not identify a specific rule number or jurisdiction.
qs: The rules require that if you enter into this limited scope arrangement, the scope must be reasonable, and the client must understand and give informed consent.
Limited scope can’t leave the client worse off than if they had no assistance.
The judge generally has to be made aware of the limited scope arrangement.

kp.k: In-house AI adoption pressures firms toward greater efficiency
kp.d: Brescia asserts that corporate legal departments are bringing more work in-house using AI, while AI companies market directly to those departments. He expects resulting client pressure on large firms to make services faster, more effective and less costly. He cites no adoption statistics or quantified savings, and the speakers acknowledge that AI-generated hallucinations also reach firms from the buyer side.
qs: There’s going to be pressure on large law firms to adopt tools to make work more efficient and effective. In-house offices are bringing more work in-house using generative AI and other AI tools.
Some large AI companies are marketing directly to in-house counsel departments, saying, we can help you bring more work in-house.
But we can look for efficiencies, make work go faster, be less costly to clients. There’s going to be pressure from clients.

kp.k: Current generative AI supports drafts, not unchecked final work
kp.d: Brescia describes generative AI as useful for first drafts, outlines, arguments and brainstorming under human supervision. His personal examples include an incorrect summary of his own paper and a useful 14-week syllabus generated in minutes for rural practitioners in upstate New York, which he would not use without further work. These are anecdotes, not benchmark findings. Lambert recommends learning the tools on material lawyers already know well so they can identify strengths and errors.
qs: People are using generative AI to produce first drafts of documents. That’s all it’s good for right now, not last drafts.
I asked a tool, give me a summary of the paper I wrote. And it was wrong. I only knew because I wrote the underlying document.
In minutes, it produced 14 weeks of subject matter. It was amazing. Would I take it and say, OK students, here’s the course? No. But it was a head start.

kp.k: Verification is basic competence, including commercial research tools
kp.d: Brescia argues that lawyers must independently establish that cited laws and cases exist and support the propositions asserted. He reports research showing hallucinations in commercial legal research systems but supplies no study name or error rate. Drawing on inherited briefs from his legal-aid practice, he emphasizes that checking original sources predates AI. Gebauer attributes failures to laziness and unchecked citations; Brescia agrees but does not offer a systematic study of causes.
qs: Research shows even the databases maintained by commercial legal research companies that use AI can hallucinate.
It’s minimum competence. You need to check that the laws you’re citing exist, the cases are real, and they say what you say they say.
You can use these tools as a head start, an outline, some arguments, maybe even cases you wouldn’t find otherwise, but you have to do the background research and make sure it’s accurate.

kp.k: Client-generated research and judicial reuse can propagate hallucinations
kp.d: Brescia describes clients bringing AI-generated research and expectations to lawyers, illustrating this with Michael Cohen’s forwarding of fabricated authorities; he expresses uncertainty about which tool Cohen used. He also discusses Mata v. Avianca, where lawyers supplied fabricated opinions as well as citations. He warns that judicial reuse can give fabricated material apparent legitimacy and says his earlier warning about judges citing hallucinated cases has materialized, without identifying the subsequent incidents.
qs: Clients are coming to lawyers saying, I did research on ChatGPT and I think I can win. Here are the cases.
The judge added an appendix with the cases as presented by the lawyers, because the lawyers submitted not only citations, but appended opinions.
There’s risk of wasting judicial and litigant resources tracking down fake cases, but the bigger risk is they get transmogrified by a judge citing them, then they look legitimate.

kp.k: Commoditization may expand provision into unmet legal markets
kp.d: Asked about the next three to five years, Brescia predicts more affordable, commoditized legal services rather than the profession’s disappearance. He applies Christensen’s disruptive-innovation mechanism: incumbents cede lower-end demand, then new providers expand as technology and delivery improve. Endorsing Richard Susskind’s latent-market framing, he states that ninety-three percent of low-income people and roughly fifty percent of middle-income people in America face legal problems without a lawyer, with cost a main reason. No underlying study or measurement period is supplied. He presents effective provision at scale by firms, companies, individuals or nonprofits as an access-to-justice and market opportunity, not an established outcome.
qs: I think we’re going to see more TurboTaxification, creating more commoditized legal services that are less expensive, easier to deliver, and satisfy clients’ jobs to be done.
When new technologies come online, incumbent firms tend to cede the lower end of a market.
Ninety-three percent of low-income people and roughly fifty percent of middle-income people in America face legal problems without a lawyer. One main reason is cost.
The entity that figures out how to deliver meaningful, effective legal services at scale will tap a blue-ocean opportunity where legal services providers don’t exist now.

kp.k: Legal education should prioritize interdisciplinary service-system design
kp.d: Brescia recommends that law schools teach technology’s capabilities, risks and benefits alongside the design of effective, scalable services matched to client needs. Rather than requiring every student to learn coding, he favors partnerships in which lawyers understand technology and engineers learn legal workflows and ethical obligations. He presents such collaboration as essential to Lawyer 3.0, not as a measured educational intervention.
qs: Help people understand the technology, the risks and benefits, and how to create systems that deliver effective legal services at scale, “just in time,” “just enough” services that address jobs to be done.

I don’t think every student should take coding for lawyers. I think students should partner with people who code, and educate engineers on how law offices work and what ethical obligations lawyers have.
Those interdisciplinary partnerships are essential for Lawyer 3.0.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Brescia predicts significant professional change, rather than the disappearance of lawyers, with AI supporting more efficient work and increasing pressure on outside firms.
pts.d: Ray Brescia describes generative AI and predictive analytics as a new inflection point in legal practice. He says generative AI is already used for first drafts, that corporate legal departments are bringing more work in-house with AI, and that AI companies market directly to those departments. He expects client pressure on large firms to increase efficiency and reduce costs. His account is primarily augmentation: AI provides a starting point, not a final work product.

pts.k: Brescia predicts more standardized, lower-cost legal services delivered at scale, opening previously underserved markets.
pts.d: He anticipates a 'TurboTaxification' of legal services: standardized products address straightforward needs, with more complex matters referred to lawyers. This prediction concerns technology-enabled delivery broadly, including expert systems, not exclusively generative AI. He expects early movers to succeed and technology-enabled providers to expand from the lower end of the market as their capabilities improve. He links this opportunity to unmet civil legal needs among low- and middle-income Americans, rather than merely enterprise cost savings.

pts.k: Brescia says AI introduces unreliable material into legal work, making human verification essential and creating risks beyond individual filings.
pts.d: He reports that clients supply AI-generated research and that commercial legal research AI can also hallucinate. He warns that fabricated authorities waste judicial and litigant resources and can acquire apparent legitimacy when judges cite them. He states that this judicial propagation has already happened, without naming a specific judicial example. His recommended response is source-level verification, including checking that authorities exist and support the asserted propositions.

pts.k: Brescia argues that next-wave legal education should prepare lawyers to design technology-enabled services through interdisciplinary collaboration.
pts.d: This is a prescription accompanying his delivery-model forecast, rather than a measured educational outcome. He calls for students to understand technological capabilities, risks and benefits, and to collaborate with engineers on systems that provide appropriately scoped services at scale. He explicitly distinguishes collaboration with coders from requiring every law student to learn coding.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Brescia supports current-use and reliability claims with personal experience, legal incidents and unspecified research, not quantified performance evaluations.
pts.d: He describes daily tool use, an inaccurate summary of his own paper, and a useful draft syllabus produced in minutes. These are contrasting personal examples of fallibility and productivity. He cites Mata v. Avianca and recounts Michael Cohen forwarding fabricated authorities to lawyers; Brescia qualifies his recollection of which tool Cohen used. His reference to research on commercial legal research tools gives no study name, methodology or error rate. Statements about insourcing and vendor marketing are observations without named departments, adoption figures or measured savings.

pts.k: The scaling forecast draws on an existing expert-system example, market-need figures and conceptual analogies rather than measured AI-driven market outcomes.
pts.d: Brescia presents Pro Bono Net’s Citizenship Works as an existing model for eligibility screening, form generation and referral when complications arise. This is an expert-system example, not evidence of generative-AI performance. He cites unmet-need percentages without a source, date or methodological explanation. He draws on Christensen’s jobs-to-be-done and disruptive-innovation frameworks and explicitly endorses Susskind’s latent-market proposition. His historical comparison with earlier technological transformations frames the forecast but does not establish its future magnitude.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Brescia distinguishes present, limited AI usefulness from a medium-term delivery forecast, without committing to precise adoption dates or magnitudes.
pts.d: Insourcing, first-draft use, client-generated research and hallucination risks are described as current developments. He says the profession is roughly three years into generative AI. His commoditization forecast answers a question about the next three to five years, but he does not supply a specific deadline, market share or savings estimate. Current usefulness depends on checking outputs and conducting underlying research; he does not endorse direct reliance on unverified AI work.

pts.k: Scaled services are conditional on suitable cases, accurate intake, escalation of complications and sufficient volume to recover development costs.
pts.d: Brescia’s standardized-service model applies to needs that a simpler product can adequately satisfy, with risks explained and bespoke alternatives available. In the Citizenship Works example, users must answer accurately and honestly for red-flag screening to work. His economic claim is that expensive initial development can be recouped over time through volume; no cost or break-even estimate is provided. For limited-scope services, his broader delivery discussion requires reasonable scope, informed consent and avoiding harm to the client.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes affect corporate buyers, incumbent firms, underserved individuals, courts, service-delivery organizations and legal educators in different ways.
pts.d: Corporate legal departments may retain more work internally, while large outside firms face pressure to deliver faster and at lower cost. Individuals with straightforward matters may obtain standardized assistance; those with complications still need expert lawyers. Low- and middle-income people with unmet civil legal needs constitute the principal proposed expansion market. Firms, companies, individuals and nonprofits capable of delivering effective services at scale may gain opportunities; Brescia does not limit that opportunity to any particular provider structure. Lawyers retain responsibility for verification, and courts and litigants bear the costs of fabricated authorities. Law schools, students and engineers are asked to collaborate on service-system design.
